result:
It means the two branches you're merging share no common ancestor commit, so git has no base to compare them against and refuses by default. The usual cause is a local repo started with `git init` and a remote that was created separately with its own first commit (a README or licence added on GitHub), and then `git pull` tries to join them.

If you do want to combine the two histories, tell git to allow it:

```
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
```

Replace `main` with your branch name, resolve any conflicts (often just the README), then commit and push. The flag works the same on `git merge`.

Before you do, run `git remote -v` to check that the remote is the repository you meant, because this error also appears when the remote points at the wrong project, and merging then would mix two unrelated codebases. If you'd rather the remote's history simply win and your local commits don't matter, re-cloning is cleaner than merging.
